shared: Essentially nothing in common: GPU ant-colony optimization for TSP versus cross-paradigm EEG classification.
Essentially nothing in common: tensorized metaheuristics for TSP versus Gaussian representation learning for medical actions.
Essentially nothing in common: parallel ant colony optimization versus Transformer-based TCR–peptide binding.
Essentially nothing in common: GPU algorithm acceleration versus influenza phylodynamics.
Essentially nothing in common: combinatorial optimization versus multi-agent clinical interview training.
Only a superficial ‘planning’ resemblance: TSP path search versus detecting action-interface uncertainty in a frozen world model. No shared problem, data, or method family.
Essentially nothing in common: evolutionary computation versus one-step flow-map supervision and uncertainty.
Essentially nothing in common: GPU ant-colony optimization versus retinal lesion segmentation.
Essentially nothing in common: combinatorial optimization versus hallucination-aware medical education.
Both are spatiotemporal representation-learning systems for medical AI: time–frequency EEG dynamics versus medical motion dynamics.
Both treat robustness and cross-distribution generalization as a central goal (cross-paradigm / cross-subject versus cross-dataset and spatiotemporal noise).
Both use purpose-built multi-stream architectures rather than off-the-shelf classifiers.
Both learn representations on biomedical data and emphasize generalization under distribution shift (cross-paradigm EEG versus de novo peptides / dataset bias).
Both use attention-style interaction to highlight salient patterns, but the domains and modalities are otherwise far apart.
Essentially nothing in common: EEG-based BCI classification versus influenza phylogeography.
A shared medical-application setting only: robust neural-signal recognition versus clinical interview training. Methods and modalities differ.
Both work with sequential observations and ask whether a model remains reliable under variability (EEG non-stationarity versus actuation shift).
The problem settings differ: discriminative classification versus uncertainty detection in a frozen world model.
Both have a medical application (BCI versus brain MRI) and a reliability concern, but one is discriminative cross-paradigm robustness and the other is generative calibration of one-step samples.
Both are medical-AI systems for perceiving fine structure that is easy to miss: salient neural patterns in noisy EEG, and tiny irregular retinal lesions.
Both introduce architectures specialized to structured biomedical data (pyramid time–frequency attention versus deformable non-causal state-space scanning).
A shared medical context only: robust EEG classification versus teaching medical students to verify generative AI.
Both learn task-specific representations in biomedical settings and introduce large curated benchmarks (CPREVAL-6K and TCRC-200k), with a shared concern for robustness.
The tasks and modalities are otherwise far apart: medical action video/skeleton analysis versus TCR–peptide binding. A real but weak link.
A shared biomedical-application setting only: clinical motion assessment versus influenza epidemiology. Data and methods barely overlap.
Both address clinical competence: GaussMedAct scores medical action quality (e.g. CPR); Agent-MedU trains and assesses clinical interviewing.
Both put process quality at the center (fine-grained clinical labels and motion errors; communication, empathy, and history-taking) rather than a single end-point label.
The methods differ, and one is primarily assessment while the other is training, but both make clinical skill observable and scorable.
Both take action as the object of study: scoring whether a medical action is correct and fine-grained, versus quantifying how far an executed action departs from the command.
Both are visual / spatiotemporal models that treat uncertainty explicitly (anisotropic covariance and noise robustness; a shift score with Cramér–Rao error bars).

Both are medical-vision papers that care about not washing out variation: anisotropic covariance of medical motion and robustness to spatiotemporal noise, versus the uncertainty and calibration that one-step samples should carry.
The technical sense of uncertainty is not the same (motion covariance versus calibrated sample spread). The shared ground is reliability in medical vision.
Both are medical computer-vision systems, aimed at fine structure that is easy to miss (subtle action errors; microaneurysms spanning a few pixels).
Both introduce modules adapted to the structure of the data (anisotropic Gaussians and dual-stream spatial encoding; deformable state-space scanning).
Adjacent clinical-training settings: scoring medical actions versus teaching students to audit AI explanations. One is a vision model, the other an educational intervention.
Both sit in computational biology around host–pathogen biology: TCR recognition of peptides, including pathogen-derived ones, versus host-mediated evolution and spread of influenza.
Both take biological sequences as primary evidence (TCR/peptide sequences versus viral genomes) and ask how host-side factors shape the outcome.
The method families differ (deep Transformers versus phylodynamics), so the overlap is scientific rather than algorithmic.
Both use large sequence models (Transformers / LLMs) in a biomedical setting, but one predicts molecular binding and the other trains clinical interviews.
Essentially nothing in common: TCR–peptide binding prediction versus action uncertainty in a frozen world model.
Essentially nothing in common: bias-aware TCR binding models versus uncertainty calibration in one-step flow maps.
Both are biomedical machine-learning systems with architectures adapted to data geometry (property cross-mapping versus deformable scanning), but the modality and task differ.
Essentially nothing in common: TCR–peptide binding versus hallucination-aware learning in medical education.
A shared health setting only: influenza epidemiology and surveillance versus clinical interview training.
Essentially nothing in common: influenza phylogeography versus robotic visual planning.
Only a weak biomedical link: Isthmus is applied to brain MRI, while H7 is influenza epidemiology. No shared method or question.
A shared biomedical-application setting only: infectious-disease epidemiology versus diabetic-retinopathy imaging.
A shared health setting only: public-health influenza spread versus AI verification in medical education.
Both take uncertainty as part of the problem: interviewing and revising hypotheses under uncertainty versus quantifying and correcting action-interface uncertainty.
The link is conceptual; one is an educational RCT, the other a statistical detector in robotic planning.

Both appear in a medical setting (clinical training versus MRI reconstruction) and care whether model outputs are trustworthy, but one is pedagogical scaffolding and the other is generative calibration.
A shared medical-AI application setting only: clinical interview training versus retinal lesion segmentation.
Both study generative AI in medical education: a multi-agent LLM standardized patient with scaffolding, and controlled exposure to AI hallucinations to train verification and trust.

Both evaluate the intervention in randomized trials with medical students, and both care about process (communication, empathy, critical thinking, reflective trust) rather than inflating knowledge or diagnostic end-points.

Both confront how AI should be used in high-stakes medical learning: Agent-MedU withholds diagnoses and refuses to inflate diagnostic accuracy; HAL documents a verification gap that persists even with warnings.
Together they form a complementary line: how to train clinical skills with AI, and how to teach learners to audit AI.
The shared core is uncertainty itself: measuring and correcting action-interface uncertainty versus restoring the uncertainty and calibration that one-step generative samples should carry.

Both keep the network (and, in Isthmus, the loss and inference code) unchanged, and change how the model is queried or supervised (reading a frozen world model backwards; a 5% isthmus that bridges a supervision island).
Both evaluate reliability and stability rather than point accuracy alone (detection AUROC, error bars, recovered success; calibration, correlation with multi-step samples, seed stability).
Both rely on a generative predictive mechanism: a world model of future observations, and a one-step flow map.
Both are visual models, but one is robotic visual planning under action uncertainty and the other is medical image segmentation. Beyond that the overlap is limited.
Both study when a model’s outputs cannot be trusted: detecting an actuation shift and correcting after an alarm, versus detecting mechanistically wrong explanations and training people to audit them.

Both argue that a surface residual or fluent form is not enough (residual energy mixes model error with the shift; fluent explanations can still be wrong), so a more specific verification signal or training is required.
Both are medical-imaging papers: one-step posterior sampling for brain MRI reconstruction, and segmentation of retinal lesions.
Both care about fine information that must not be washed out (uncertainty that samples should carry; tiny irregular lesions).
The methods differ (generative flow maps versus state-space segmentation).
Both concern the reliability of generative outputs: one-step samplers can lose uncertainty and become overconfident; generated explanations can be fluent and still mechanistically wrong.
Both treat calibration or verification as a necessary complement to generation, rather than assuming that generative quality implies trustworthiness.
A shared medical-application setting only: retinal lesion segmentation versus AI verification in medical education.
